en: That's nine knots, diver. I'm running out of rope.
Tie a tenth. I'm good for it.
Then you can untie three. Sit. Eat.
Gulls have been quiet all morning.
Sabe, they're carved. They're always quiet.
Wind's at our backs, that's why. Wood only talks when the sea does.
Not a cloud since dawn. I don't like it.
You don't like rain either. You don't like anything.
The Other Mender
I like a sky that's honest about what it wants.
Sallow! Come to complain about my arithmetic again?
You paid me for half a lamp-housing. I sold you a whole one.
The other half was my company. We sail at the turn.
The side went to Tamsule without me. Next year they'll have to take me.
We're winning the Tidecup this year. Tavi says.
Tavi says that every year. Keep your elbows in.
Rhen! Off the cabin roof! Ma says you used to.
I was young and foolish then. Now I'm just foolish.
Scared!
Fine. Fine. Watch how it's done.
He did it!
Morning. Don't get up.
Air's stale. Air's always stale. Four hundred years and nobody thought to open a window.
Brass in the door hinges. Somebody in the Lit Age loved a hinge.
I'll take that off your hands. You won't miss it.
Kell! Kell, the bridge!
The net-pen, Rhen! I said the net-pen! Go!
Going. I'm going.
Tide's breathing out. Right on time.
Two metres of Lit Age brass. A month of oil, if the scale-man's sober.
Come on. Come on. There.
Go! Don't look back, go!
My father used to sing the currents. I hadn't heard it in eleven years. Then nothing.
...That's the gulls.
Lines in! Everybody off the low hulls!
That's a ship. That's a whole ship, and it's wearing it.
I'm not scared. I'm busy.
Sallow. Over here. Second dive?
Tide's good, and the scale-man's in a robbing mood. I need more brass.
Hand. For luck.
For luck.
Stay a minute.
Tide's turning, Kell.
Then go and catch it.
Then make yourself useful. Wicks for the afternoon divers. Even lengths.
Even lengths. I've been doing this since I was eight.
Badly. Since you were eight, badly. Give those here.
Kell. Why did you never learn to swim?
Never needed to. The sea owes me a favour, and I've never once collected.
It can't take me while it's in debt. Salt and stone, that's plain trade.
That isn't how debt works.
It's how mine works.
Tavi asked you twice to go to Tamsule with the side. Why didn't you?
Somebody has to keep you in brass.
Hm.
Go on. The tide won't wait for a pretty face, and it won't wait for yours either.
That's the nicest thing you've said all week.
Nobody goes below the ninth floor.
You don't follow the low lights.
Every diver in Oruvel was taught that. Nobody ever told us why.
Rhen! The net's going!
I know. Hands on the plank. Don't look at the water, look at me.
Keel-hull. Go, and don't stop for anything. I'm right behind you.
Sallow. What's the sea coughed up today?
Lit Age tide-gauge. Solid brass, four hundred years old, and not one tooth missing.
Plain brass, by the pound. Forty lume.
Forty? It's not scrap, it's history. History's heavier. Check your scale.
Haggle him up.
Look at those teeth. Somebody cut every one by hand. That's sixty lume of somebody.
Fifty. Your father would've taken the first price, you know.
He never was much for arguing.
No. Quiet man. Fifty, and I'm robbing myself.
Take his price.
Forty. Fine. You'll sell it upcoast for four hundred.
Six hundred. I've a family to feed.
Unbound, by the Level. There's your chit.
Unbound, by the Level. You'd stamp the sea if it held still long enough.
I would. Off you go, diver.
What are you? No. Don't answer that.
One month earlier.
Oruvel sat on top of a drowned city. Most mornings I went down to take some of it home.
The reef's showing.
Cut the low hulls loose! Everyone to the keel-hull! Children first!
Lines in! Lines in!
Divers in the water, watch my lamp! Swim for the light!
Cast off! Sea room, all of you, find sea room!
Kell!
Not me, you fool! The net-pen! The little ones!
Go to the net-pen.
Kell first.

Hold, Rhen. No one walks the causeway without resting at the town shrine first.
It only takes a moment. Sit at the little shrine in town, then we'll go.
The Lady Cantor's shell is cut. They'll set it at the wake.
I'm sorry. Was she very old?
Mind the steps, please. I've only just swept them.
Her mother went from this dock too. Same age near enough.
Then she'll have fair weather. Her mother did.
Went where?
Out. Pass me that float, would you?
One for the shell and two for the ash,
three for the bell and four for the hush...
What comes after four?
You start again. Everybody knows that.
Two days. Two days, and she's still helping me wrap fish.
Salt and stone. Her knots are neater than mine ever were.
Who's leaving? You've wrapped enough for a whole crew.
Hold this end, would you? The leaf tears if you pull it.
The sea gave me back at dawn. Somebody was humming.
A star-path. The one they teach children for finding the way home.
There you are. No, don't sit up yet. You've swallowed half the bay.
Lie still, please, and keep your hands open. I would like this to stay a small conversation.
That's a very big spear for a very small conversation.
Toma. He's half drowned. I think he's allowed one joke.
One.
That lantern.
Where did you get it?
It was my father's.
Then it's a good thing the sea gave you both back.
Good trade. Don't ask what I gave for it.
Then I won't ask. Not today.
Rhen Sallow. Oruvel, the raft-town, east of here, all those ugly hulls tied together. Is it still there?
We watched the storm go east last night. I am sorry.
The water's thick this morning.
Those are ours. Aren't they.
Some of them came in with you. I heard them on the water before it was light.
She woke the house before light. We came down so they would not come ashore alone.
Stay with them a minute.
Mother Kell can't swim. Never learned. Said the sea owed her a favour.
You don't have to be anything yet. Not on this beach.
Be level, Oruvel.
Don't look at them. Get up.
No. Up. I'm getting up. The beach is moving, but I'm getting up.
Slowly.
Lean on him. He likes it, he just won't say so.
I'm Asha. That's Toma. He's nicer than his spear.
Toma Okeru, of Haluna. You are speaking to the Lady—
To Asha. Who is very glad you aren't dead.
Lady what?
Later. You're shaking.
Come up to the village. Bring your father's light. You'll eat first, and then we'll tell you what we know.
Come up to the village. You'll eat first, and then we'll tell you what we know.
She smiled first. Every time. It took me a long while to understand why.
Every roof's got one, and every one faces the sea. Nobody carves a gull to watch the land.
Once we cross, we won't be back before dark. Is there anyone you want to see first?
Go now.
Not yet.
Then go and see them. The tide will hold a while yet.
The tide-readers set the day. The causeway opens this far twice a month.
Come and see it, Rhen. It's the most beautiful thing we have.
He is not sworn to anything, Asha.
I know. I'm already walking, Toma.
Up, then. Sit. Not that stool, it bites.
Fish, then bread, then more fish. The sea gave you back thin.
That's a lot of food for one stranger.
It's the right amount. Eat. Asha's at the market. She'll want to show you everything today.
They don't need two washings, diver. Go on. She'll be waiting at the causeway.
Mind the bowl. That's fresh water, and it came a long way.
Here, let me. I've scrubbed worse off a hull. ...That one was already clean, wasn't it?
With the ridges, not against them. Gently. You'd wash a face that way.
There. Shoulder height, clean-edged. Nobody is in that one yet.
And this one I can find with my eyes shut. Teyo Marrin.
Family?
My grandmother Pila's big brother. He went as Cantor at sixteen, so the Order would take him and not her. She was the stronger hearer.
He was frightened the whole way. Grandmother said he went anyway.
And Pila?
Lived to ninety-one. Mended nets to the end, and never once sang. Not even to children, in case anyone was listening.
Salt and stone. Ninety-one years of not singing.
You'll go up to the shrine with her? Say hello to him for us.
To who?
That one's snapped clean through. Nobody's put up a new one?
Nobody mends the posts.
Why not?
Mind the shells, Rhen. They cut.
There's light in that crack. Lit Age ceramic, still lit. That's a month of food, sitting in the sand.
Leave it.
...Leaving it.
Look. Star-snail, comb-anemone, and a little lamp-crab under the ledge.
Two copper, nothing, and four if you catch him before he sheds.
Is that all a pool is to a diver? A price on every shell?
The anemone was free. I'm not a monster.
Guardian. Keep her feet dry and her lamp lit. That's the whole of the rite.
I can do that.
Fair weather to you, diver. Bring her back the long way round.
The long way. I'll remember.
Are you going with the Lady? Then you have to learn the rhyme.
Teach me tomorrow.
So you're the one walking with her. Take the dried fish. All of it.
I'll carry it for both of us.
Asha. On the shrine steps, Toma said...
How was your day, Rhen? Truly.
...Long. Good, mostly.
You leave the day after tomorrow.
At first tide. The causeway won't wait for me.
Then let me come. As your guardian. I can dive, and I can carry, and I don't scare.
Yes.
Asha. A guardian is not chosen on a dock, at night—
This one was, Toma.
Then you walk behind me.
Don't look so worried, both of you. It's only my first one.
Shout if it bites.
He's been in there a hundred and forty years. I think he'll be polite.
We will be here, Lady Cantor.
Toma.
...Asha.
So. How long does a verse take?
As long as it takes. The last time, the village waited on the beach until dark.
You weren't here for that one?
I was at Ansedra then, at the temples. I heard of it by letter.
Do you ever put that spear down?
To eat.
Do you know what a Cantor is?
...Someone who sings?
Yes. Someone who sings.
And then she comes home?
Then the storm sleeps. For years. Children grow up who have never seen it.
That's not an answer.
No. It is not.
Seems like a lot of fuss for one song.
You do not mock the rites, Rhen. You may ask about them. That is different.
I'm asking. Badly, but I'm asking.
Then ask her. Not me. She has earned the telling of it.
I have guarded her three years. Before that, on leave, I had to find her in the net racks. She hid on purpose.
And now?
Now she does not hide. I find I miss it.
This morning, in the water. You stayed with them.
Somebody should have.
Yes. I think so too.
Oh. It's evening.
You're glowing. Is that normal? Toma, is that normal?
It is normal.
It tickles.
Was it him? The boy from the shells. Teyo.
He's still frightened. He was kind to me anyway.
He was kind to me. I didn't expect that.
Found this in the side pool. Seemed like it belonged to someone.
He carries one just like it.
Keep it. I think he'd like it to stay with someone who goes home.
The verse. It is sung toward home first.
I know, Toma. I watched it once.
Vey ennu, vey ennu,
hal oan, ish karra.
Ennu re, ennu re...
...mir.
...where did you learn that?
Just now. It's the first verse.
Rhen?
My father hummed that. Every night.
Every night until he didn't.
My mother hummed it to me every night, and sang it from this door. I was seven. I'd forgotten it until tonight.
...He never said where he learned it.
Nowhere. Must have been the wind.
All right. Not today.
That's twice you haven't answered me, Rhen Sallow. I'm patient.
The tide has turned.
Something heard that.
On my shield. Everyone, on my shield, now.
Start at the spring. Follow the water, not the stone.
Everyone I'm going to tell you about is still here tonight. Remember that, later.
